summary: Defines a way for a SIP user agent and its next-hop SIP server to negotiate which security mechanism they will use. It supplements existing ways of choosing security between SIP entities. It was later updated by RFC 8996.

eli5.summary: Before whispering a secret, two people need to agree on a code. This document lets two phone systems agree on which kind of protection to use before they talk.

questions: how do sip entities negotiate security mechanisms
how do sip entities negotiate security
subtitle: A secure way for a SIP phone and its first-hop server to agree on how to protect their conversation.

tldr.problem: If two SIP peers pick a security mechanism from unprotected offers, a man-in-the-middle can strip out the strong options and force weak security.
tldr.mechanism: The client lists its mechanisms, the server answers with its own list, the client switches on the best common one and then repeats the server's list over the now-protected channel so the server can check it was not changed.
tldr.outcome: Networks can move from, say, HTTP Digest to IPsec or TLS without upgrading every device at once. RFC 8996 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 3329 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 8996; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Negotiate Security
sections.content:
Security protocols traditionally include a way to agree on mechanisms and algorithms, because different mechanisms suit different situations and old ones get retired. This RFC defines such a negotiation for SIP, intended to work only between a user agent and its first-hop SIP entity.

Without a secured way to choose, SIP is open to attacks. Authentication and integrity protection with several alternative methods is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks, and it can be hard to tell whether a mechanism is truly unavailable to the peer or an attack is under way. The RFC says SIP was expected to reach hundreds of millions of small devices with little chance of coordinated policies or software upgrades, so negotiation had to exist from the start.

Its design goals are: find the exact mechanisms to apply without excessive round trips, make the selection itself secure, let the parties signal success or failure, and avoid adding state to be maintained.
sections.eli5: Little devices cannot all be updated at once, so they need a safe way to agree on protection from the very beginning.

sections.title: The Five-Step Flow
sections.content:
The overall exchange has five steps:

  1. The client sends a list of its supported security mechanisms along with its first request.
  2. The server challenges the client and sends the mechanisms and parameters it supports.
  3. The client selects the highest-preference mechanism they have in common and turns it on.
  4. The client contacts the server again using that mechanism, and returns the server's list.
  5. The server checks the returned list against its own to make sure it was not modified.

The procedure is stateless for servers unless the chosen mechanism itself needs state. Both lists are static: they do not and cannot change based on what the other side sends. A node may keep several static lists, for example one per interface.
sections.eli5: Shout your list, hear their list, pick the best match, then say their list back using the new secret code. If it matches, all is well.

sections.title: The Three New Header Fields
sections.content:
The RFC defines three header fields: Security-Client, Security-Server and Security-Verify. Each holds a comma-separated list of mechanisms, and each mechanism is a name plus optional parameters.

Four mechanism names are defined: tls (TLS), digest (HTTP Digest), ipsec-ike (IPsec with IKE) and ipsec-man (manually keyed IPsec without IKE). The parameter q gives a preference; higher is preferred, and all mechanisms MUST have different q values.

Three further parameters apply only to HTTP Digest and exist to prevent bidding-down attacks: d-alg (the digest algorithm), d-qop (the quality of protection) and d-ver, a quoted 32-digit hex value that protects the Security-Server header field itself. Whitespace in Security-Server MUST be reduced to single spaces before the d-ver value is calculated or checked. The RFC stresses that it makes no change to HTTP Digest, only reuses it to protect the negotiation.
sections.eli5: There are three labelled boxes: one for what the client can do, one for what the server can do, and one for the server's list repeated back to check it.

sections.title: Client and Server Procedures
sections.content:
Client initiated. A client that wants to use this mechanism adds a Security-Client header field to a request addressed to its first-hop proxy, plus both Require and Proxy-Require with the value sec-agree. It SHOULD NOT add preference parameters. A server receiving an unprotected request with those headers MUST answer 494 (Security Agreement Required) with a Security-Server list, even if there is no common mechanism, and that list MUST NOT depend on the client's list.

The client then picks the mechanism with the highest q value among those it knows and starts it. Later requests SHOULD use that mechanism and MUST carry a Security-Verify header field mirroring the server's list, along with Require and Proxy-Require. The server compares it with its static list; both lists must have the same mechanisms in the same order with the same parameter values. If the list was modified, the server MUST respond 494 again with its unmodified list. If it matches and the server is a proxy, it removes sec-agree from Require and Proxy-Require. The user of the UA SHOULD be told about the result.

Server initiated. A server decides based on local policy. If it sees more than one Via entry it is not the first hop, MUST NOT use the mechanism, and returns 502 (Bad Gateway). A server that requires the mechanism and sees no sec-agree option tag in Require, Proxy-Require or Supported MUST return 421 (Extension Required); if the tag was in Supported it MUST return 494. Either response includes Security-Server and a Require header with sec-agree. Clients that support the extension SHOULD add sec-agree to a Supported header field.
sections.eli5: The client says, "I would like to agree on protection." The server must reply with its own list. After switching on the protection, the client repeats the server's list so the server can spot any change.

sections.title: Starting the Chosen Mechanism
sections.content:
Each mechanism starts differently. For tls, the client treats a SIP URI as if it were sips and follows the SIP server-location procedures; if the scheme is not sip, the request MUST be sent over TLS. For digest, the 494 response carries a Digest challenge, and the client MUST replace the algorithm and qop parameters in that challenge with those from Security-Server and MUST use the d-ver value in Security-Verify. For ipsec-ike, the client tries to set up an IKE connection to the host part of the Request-URI, and a failed attempt means the agreement has failed and MUST be terminated. For ipsec-man, the peers must already know the keys; how they learn them is out of scope.

The RFC also says how long the agreement lasts. With TLS, closing the connection means a new negotiation is needed. IKE negotiates the lifetime. With Digest, the server re-challenges when credentials stop being valid. With ipsec-man, the same out-of-band mechanism that distributes keys is assumed to define the duration.
sections.eli5: Each kind of protection has its own way to switch on, and its own way of saying when it has run out and needs to be set up again.

sections.title: Compatibility with Older Clients
sections.content:
Use of this extension is a matter of local policy and may differ per network interface. Both UA and server implementations MUST be configurable to work with or without it. A server using the mechanism may also accept clients that use TLS under the normal SIP rules.

A client that supports neither this extension nor TLS cannot be accepted, which breaks interoperability with some SIP clients. The RFC therefore advises using it where every client either implements the extension or can use TLS, or where refusing to communicate is preferable to insecure communication.
sections.eli5: If someone does not know the secret handshake at all, they cannot come in. That is fine only if everyone you want to talk to knows it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The method is secure only if the weakest proposed mechanism offers at least integrity and replay protection for the Security-Verify header field. The core point is downgrade resistance. If offers are unprotected, any attacker can remove the strong options and push both peers to weak security. With the repeat-the-list design, the attacker must modify both the offer and the later message, and must forge the weak security in real time, otherwise the hash will not match.

The RFC walks through attacks. Changing the server's list in the first response is revealed when the client returns it over the chosen security. Changing the repeated list is blocked by encryption or detected through integrity protection. Changing the client's list cannot alter the client's own choice, and if it changes the server's choice the two end up with mismatched mechanisms and treat it as a possible attack. Replaying old messages must be stopped by each mechanism; for Digest this means careful use of nonces and nonce counters. All clients MUST select HTTP Digest, TLS, IPsec or something stronger to protect the second request.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person could cross out the best code from the list. But since the list is repeated later using the chosen code, the change gets caught.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC creates a new registry of mechanism names. It registers digest, tls, ipsec-ike, ipsec-man and also ipsec-3gpp, which is described in Appendix A. Further names are allocated by IETF Consensus and need a published RFC.

It also registers three header fields (Security-Client, Security-Server, Security-Verify, none with a compact form), the response code 494 (Security Agreement Required), and the option tag sec-agree.
sections.eli5: The new names, number and keyword were added to the official lists so everyone uses them the same way.
